title: Feedback is Fire (But LOTS of Teachers Misunderstand and Overcomplicate It) ercomplicate-it
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart distills feedback theory into three non-negotiable traits — it has to be quick, intelligible, and manageable — and argues that if even one is missing, feedback's power to help a learner collapses. He then makes the case that in-the-moment verbal feedback (looking over shoulders while students draft a paragraph, listening in on paired discussion, interrupting a pop-up debate to coach a skill live) consistently outperforms delayed, written feedback like a next-day rubric, precisely because it satisfies all three traits at once. That conviction is strong enough that Stuart says he has stopped grading pop-up debates with a rubric altogether, relying instead on real-time coaching. He closes by tying feedback back to two other principles from his forthcoming course — practice and testing — arguing neither works without a feedback loop that tells students how their practice is going and what their results mean.
points: Stuart operationalizes "good feedback" into three testable traits — quick, intelligible, manageable — giving teachers a checklist rather than a vague ideal to aim for.
He names a specific exception to the speed requirement: late feedback on a long-term project can still land because the student has thought about the work enough to reconstruct context.

In-the-moment verbal feedback during live tasks (pop-up debates, paired review) is positioned as strictly more effective than delayed written rubrics because it satisfies all three feedback traits simultaneously.
Stuart reports having abandoned rubric-based grading for pop-up debates entirely in favor of real-time coaching, a concrete practice change driven directly by this feedback framework.
quotes: It's gotta be quick — if I've forgotten what I was thinking when I did the thing I'm getting feedback on, I'll be unlikely to use the feedback. It's gotta be intelligible — if it doesn't make sense to me, I'll be unable to use it.
When even one of these traits is absent, the helpfulness of feedback dwindles rapidly.
By far the most effective method of feedback I employ as a teacher, then, is in-the-moment feedback on what students are working on.

As my students discuss unit review questions in pairs, I walk around, listen in, and give verbal feedback to help them hone their answers, illustrate concepts with concrete details, or clarify vague thinking.
This kind of feedback is so effective, in fact, that I've long done away with grading pop-up debates with a rubric.
The in-the-moment feedback is so much more powerful than the next day rubric because it's 1) timely, 2) intelligible, and 3) manageable.
For both of these applications of the science of learning, they need to know how the practice is going and what to make of their test results. For both of these, they'll need feedback.
